title: A Wall of Trees Across Africa
intro: In 2007, African countries began an ambitious project to stop the spread of the desert. The plan has changed a great deal since then.

passage: The Sahel is a long belt of dry land that stretches across Africa just south of the Sahara Desert, from the Atlantic coast in the west to the Red Sea in the east. Tens of millions of people live there, and most of them depend on farming and keeping animals. Over the past half-century, however, the region has faced severe droughts, a growing population and increasing pressure on the land. In many places, soil that once produced crops has become dry and dusty, a process known as land degradation.

In 2007, the African Union launched an ambitious response: the Great Green Wall. The original idea was simple and easy to imagine – a line of trees around 15 kilometres wide and roughly 8,000 kilometres long, running across the continent from Senegal to Djibouti. Eleven countries joined the initiative at the start, and the number involved has since grown. Like a giant natural barrier, the trees would stop the desert from moving south, protect farmland and provide wood, fruit and shade. The project quickly attracted international attention and promises of financial support.

It soon became clear, however, that planting trees in such a harsh environment was far from easy. In some countries, millions of seedlings were planted, but a large proportion of them died within a few years because they did not receive enough water or care. Some of the species chosen were not suited to local conditions, and in some areas local people had not been consulted, so they had little reason to protect the young trees. A wall of trees, critics argued, could not simply be built from the outside.

As a result, the project gradually changed its approach. Instead of a single line of trees, the Great Green Wall is now described as a mosaic of different projects, each designed to restore damaged land in ways that suit local communities. The goals have also grown: by 2030, the initiative aims to restore 100 million hectares of land and to create millions of jobs in rural areas. Trees are still important, but so are water management, rules about grazing and sustainable farming.

Some of the most successful methods are surprisingly cheap. In Niger, many farmers no longer plant new trees; instead, they protect the shoots that grow naturally from old tree roots and stumps in their fields. In Burkina Faso, farmers dig small pits in hard ground and fill them with compost before the rainy season, so that water and nutrients collect around the seeds. One farmer, Yacouba Sawadogo, became known around the world for using this method over several decades to turn bare land into a forest. These traditional techniques have helped to bring life back to land that many people had considered useless.

Progress overall, though, has been slower than many had hoped. An assessment published by the United Nations in 2020 suggested that only a small fraction of the target had been reached, partly because of a lack of money and partly because of conflict and insecurity in several countries along the route. Measuring success is also difficult, as restored land is spread across a huge area and is not always easy to monitor. Some critics also argue that too much attention was paid to the number of trees planted rather than the number that survived.

Despite these difficulties, supporters believe that the Great Green Wall has changed the way people think about the desert. The lesson, they say, is that environmental projects work best when local people are involved and benefit directly, for example by selling fruit, honey or other products from restored land. If that lesson is learned, the wall may never look like the one that was first imagined, but it could still transform the lives of millions of people.
